title: Loss and exile close
hookLine: a lost kingdom, a lost boy, a found faith

lines: A DIAMOND SENT ACROSS THE SEA.
cards: A great diamond, sent across the sea to a queen: the Koh-i-Noor, taken from a boy king and never given back. But there's an older jewel in this story, and nobody could put it in a box.

Guru Nanak names it in the Japji: within the mind, he says, are jewels, gems and rubies, if a person listens to the Guru's teaching even once. A diamond can be taken. That jewel, the Japji says, is within.

teach.b: A kingdom lost. This stretch began with nirbhau: Mudki and Ferozeshah, then Sobraon and a sense of betrayal, a treaty that gave away Kashmir, a queen sent away from her son.

Then Multan rose, the army held at Chillianwala, lost at Gujrat, and Punjab was annexed. A boy lost. Duleep Singh was raised by British guardians, baptized a Christian, and settled at Elveden, far from Punjab.
He met his mother again after long years apart, and she told him who he was. She died in London, and he carried her body toward home.
A faith found again. Stopped at Aden on his way to India, Duleep took amrit. He died in Paris, an exile.
His daughters went on: Sophia marching for women's votes, Bamba keeping the family's memory in Lahore.
A people asking. Sikh soldiers served far away. Farmers moved to new canal land.

Missionaries and reformers argued, mahants held the gurdwaras' keys, and families asked who they were. Bhai Maharaj Singh, sent away to be forgotten, was remembered in Singapore. And the long question stayed open.
So much was taken: land, army, throne, diamond, a boy's childhood.
And yet the hymns, the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat were still there to come back to. Duleep came back. Sikhs kept asking.
Next comes the answer people built: a stretch of the story called reform and renewal.

how: Sikhs remember the years after the fall of the Sikh kingdom as a time of loss and exile, and tell Duleep Singh's return to Sikhi as part of how the community found its footing again.

o: a crown worn by the Maharaja at court
a jewel; the Japji finds them in the mind
a gift sent to a queen across the sea

games.q: loss and exile — tap the pairs.
p: sent across the sea to a queen
kept the family's memory in Lahore

s: he died in Paris, an exile.
stopped on his way to India, he came back to Sikhi.
the Japji says the jewels are kept in a treasury
it says they are within the mind, for one who listens to the Guru's teaching.

games.q: you're Duleep Singh, stopped at Aden, kept from going on to India. you can't reach Punjab. what do you do?
o: give up and sail back to England.
wait for permission and do nothing.
games.why: he took amrit at Aden. he never reached Punjab, but he came back to Sikhi.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you lost for a while and found again, a friendship, a faith, a habit, a part of yourself, a song, a place, and remember what it was like without it, then the moment it came back, or the slow way it returned.
Hold that return, and let it be as quiet or as warm as it is. If you pray, say Waheguru for it.

wordCard.voice: Ratan, a jewel: within the mind, the Japji says, are jewels, gems and rubies. The end of this stretch: a lost kingdom, a lost boy, and a faith found again. Today's word.

orig.note: ratan, a jewel; in the Japji, jewels, gems and rubies are within the mind.

carryVoice: Your line: found again. Lost for years, and then found, in a port at Aden. Nine hundred fifty-six days, and counting.
